thread.title: Ann Saterbak gets Fulbright Global Scholar Award to study cultural differences in engineering education
thread.title_full: Ann Saterbak gets Fulbright Global Scholar Award to study cultural differences in engineering education

author: Leena Mirchandani
title: Ann Saterbak gets Fulbright Global Scholar Award to study cultural differences in engineering education
text:
Ann Saterbak, professor of the practice in the department of biomedical engineering, was awarded the Fulbright Global Scholar Award, which will fund her new cross-cultural work in engineering education in Malawi, Singapore and Uganda.
“When I think about teaching, I think about the whys: why and how students are learning certain things,” she said.
Saterbak aims to research various successful pre-existing engineering programs in these countries, as well as how cultural differences may impact teaching styles. She described her project as “part research and part education.”
“I became curious about how and why some kinds of teaching techniques were used in different countries, different contexts, different types of classes, and it was out of that that the research evolved,” Saterbak said.
The Fulbright Global Scholar Award grants U.S. academics resources to engage in global research and teaching projects in two world regions. Academics of all disciplines and lengths of tenure are able to apply.
The Fulbright Scholars Program has faced upheaval in recent months after 11 of the 12 members of the board resigned due to interference from the Trump administration. Former board members claimed that the U.S. Department of State sent rejection letters to previously selected award recipients, including some at Duke.
“I didn't tell people for a long time because I assumed the funding was going to get pulled, but it hasn't yet,” Saterbak said. “ … At this point, I'm starting to put money down, so fingers crossed that the funding doesn't get pulled.”
The award’s funding will support Saterbak’s travel and lodging, while also providing an additional layer of security. Saterbak also felt that the award bestows her with an informal ambassadorial responsibility.
“[I will] try to liaise with the government and other people who are in the country and try to be a positive representative of the United States during a time when not everyone has a great impression of the United States,” Saterbak said.
Saterbak will partner with the Malawi University of Business and Applied Sciences to examine how they have “transformed their engineering program.” By researching these practices, Saterbak hopes to document some of their educational techniques to support other schools in Malawi.
This research aims to translate successful MUBAS practices to other universities in Malawi, allowing them to move away from “a traditional lecture-based British model to a modern Malawi model,” Saterbak said.
A key part of Saterbak’s project includes instructing teaching workshops to educators in Malawi — which she has already done for approximately 12 years — because at the end of the project, these teachers will be the ones who “stay there and do the hard work.”
Saterbak has studied the science of teaching and learning for decades, exploring the contextual and cultural elements that influence teaching techniques.
Saterbak was recruited to Duke in 2017 to develop the first-year engineering design program, which emphasizes collaboration and hands-on learning.
Saterbak hopes that her upcoming research will build on her past work to “build something that can help in a transformative way.”
